content: CYCLONE Building Basics (Cyclones) About Cyclones  In meteorological terms, a cyclone is a wind system that rotates inwards ( counter-clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern ) around a strong low-pressure centre.  Simply put, inward-spiralling winds that rotate about a low-pressure zone is known as a cyclone.  Generally, when winds rise above 118 kmph, it is known as a cyclone.  Eastern and Central North Pacific: Hurricanes  Western Northern Pacific: Typhoons  Arabian Sea/Northern Indian Ocean: Tropical Cyclones  South Indian Ocean: Tropical Cyclones/Willy-Willy for southwest Australia  Coral Sea/South Pacific: Tropical Cyclone Category Wind Speed in Km/h 1 120-150 2 150-180 3 180-210 4 210-250 5 250 and above Formation of Tropical Cyclones Tropical cyclones are intense low-pressure systems that form over warm tropical oceans and are characterized by strong winds, heavy rainfall, and spiraling thunderstorms . Their formation involves a combination of atmospheric and oceanic conditions. Stages of Tropical Cyclone Formation  Preliminary Stage – Formation of a Low-Pressure Area  Warm Ocean Waters: Sea surface temperatures above 27°C (80°F) provide the heat and moisture necessary for cyclone formation.  Evaporation and Condensation: Warm water heats the air above, causing moist air to rise. As the air ascends, it cools and condenses , releasing latent heat which fuels the cyclone. 2 PRELIMS SAMPOORNA: GEOGRAPHY  Development Stage – Cyclogenesis  Low-Pressure System Formation: Rising warm, moist air creates a region of low pressure at the surface.  Coriolis Force Impact: The Earth’s rotation (Coriolis effect) causes the winds to spiral inward in a counterclockwise direction in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere .  Convergence of Winds: Surrounding air rushes in to fill the low-pressure zone, further intensifying the system.  Mature Stage – Intensification of the Cyclone  Eye Formation: As the cyclone strengthens, a calm and clear eye forms at the center, surrounded by the most violent winds and thunderstorms (eyewall).  Symmetric Structure: Spiral rain bands form around the eye, contributing to heavy rainfall and storm surges.  Continuous Heat Cycle: Warm moist air continues to rise and release heat, intensifying wind speeds (up to 300 km/h in severe cases).  Dissipation Stage – Weakening of the Cyclone  Landfall: When the cyclone moves over land or cooler waters , it loses its energy source (Warm Ocean) and gradually weakens.  Increased Wind Shear: Strong upper-level winds disrupt the cyclone’s structure.  Cooling Ocean: Movement over cooler waters leads to a reduction in energy supply. Conditions Necessary for Tropical Cyclone Formation  Warm Ocean Temperature: Minimum 27°C up to a depth of 50 meters .  Low Vertical Wind Shear: Minimal difference in wind speed and direction with altitude.  Coriolis force: At least 5° latitude from the equator is required to initiate rotation (cyclones cannot form directly at the equator ).  Moisture in the Troposphere: High levels of humidity are needed for cloud formation and sustaining convection.  Pre-existing Disturbance: A weather disturbance like an easterly wave or low-pressure system is essential to trigger cyclogenesis.

content: Regions Prone to Tropical Cyclones Tropical cyclones form in the following cyclone basins :  North Atlantic Ocean (Hurricanes)  Northeast Pacific Ocean (Hurricanes)  Northwest Pacific Ocean (Typhoons)  Indian Ocean (Cyclones)  Southwest Pacific and Southeast Indian Ocean (Cyclones) Cyclone Warning Systems  In order to cater to the needs of Cyclone Warning Services and Marine weather services, there are seven established Cyclone Warning Centers covering the east & west coasts of our country.  Among these,  three are Area Cyclone Warning Centres (ACWCs) located at Chennai, Mumbai and Kolkata  four are Cyclone Warning Centres (CWCs) located at Ahmadabad, Thiruvananthapuram, Visakhapatnam and Bhubaneswar Advancements in cyclone tracking technology  Satellite Constellations: The Cyclone Global Navigation Satellite System (CYGNSS), launched by NASA, employs a network of eight microsatellites to measure ocean surface wind speeds. This system provides frequent observations, improving our understanding of cyclone formation and intensity. 3 IAS PRELIMS 2025  Enhanced Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP): Advances in NWP have led to more accurate cyclone track forecasts. Improved data collection and modelling techniques have increased lead times, allowing for better preparedness.  Innovative Hurricane Modeming: NOAA’s Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) represents a next- generation model aiming to provide reliable guidance on tropical cyclone track, intensity, and structure. Continuous refinements enhance prediction accuracy.  Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (Drones): The deployment of advanced drones capable of penetrating turbulent zones between air and water has provided valuable data on heat exchanges that fuel hurricanes. This real-time data enhances forecasts regarding storm trajectory, speed, and intensity.  Machine Learning Techniques: Researchers are developing machine learning models to detect and track tropical cyclones using reanalysis data. These models can efficiently process large datasets, offering accurate predictions of cyclone paths and intensities. 1 CYCLONES IN BAY OF BENGAL AND ARABIAN SEA Context: A report highlighted the increasing occurrence of Cyclones in the Arabian Sea as compared to the Bay of Bengal over several years due to climate change. The Geographic Location  Arabian Sea: The Arabian Sea is bordered by Oman, Iran, India, Pakistan and the Arabian Peninsula.  Bay of Bengal: It is bordered by India to the west, Bangladesh to the north, and Burma and Thailand to the east. What is the general trend of cyclones?  Generally, India gets 5 cyclones on an average in a year.  4 in the Bay of Bengal  1 in the Arabian Sea Bay of Bengal vs. Arabian Sea Factors affecting cyclones in the Bay of Bengal Factors affecting cyclones over the Arabian Sea  The Bay of Bengal is fed by a constant source of freshwater in the form of giant rivers like the Ganga and the Brahmaputra.  The river water that empties into the Bay of Bengal warms up at the surface and rises up as moisture.  This makes it difficult for the warm layers of water to mix properly with the cooler layers of water below, keeping the surface always warm and ready to feed any potential cyclone over it.

content:  Furthermore, because of the shape of the land around the Bay of Bengal, the winds are slower and weaker over the ocean, ready to spin.  Conversely, the northern, central, and western parts of the Arabian Sea have much cooler temperatures.  The mountains in east Africa direct winds toward the Arabian Peninsula, dissipating heat much more efficiently throughout the Arabian Sea.  As a result, this region is not favourable to feed potential cyclones, and about half the cyclones that move into this area typically lose energy and dissipate.  However, this year, the sea surface temperatures continue to remain abnormally high, in the 30s, feeding cyclonic conditions. Cyclone Hazard Zone in India  As per the Indian Meteorological Department , 13 coastal regions and Union Territories in India are prone to a cyclone.  This happens because of the long coastline of 8041 Km, which is exposed to nearly 10% of the world’s tropical cyclones. For that cause, both the coasts of India experience cyclonic storms often.  Vulnerable states- West Bengal, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Odisha, Puducherry (UT), Maharashtra, Gujarat FACT BOX Factors influencing formation & intensification of cyclones  The formation of tropical cyclones and their intensification are governed by various geophysical and thermodynamic parameters such as:  sea surface temperatures 4 PRELIMS SAMPOORNA: GEOGRAPHY  sea level pressure  tropical cyclone heat potential  convective available potential energy  air temperature at height levels  relative humidity at mid-tropospheric levels  vertical wind shear 2 IMPACT OF CYCLONE ON MONSOON’S ONSET Context: As the effect of Global warming, the occurrence of cyclones in  Indian Ocean  and typhoons in  North- western Pacific Ocean is changing, which has a significant impact on onset and withdrawal of monsoon in India. Impact of Cyclones on Monsoon’s Onset Cyclones play a significant role in influencing the onset, progression, and intensity of the Indian monsoon . Their impact varies depending on their location, timing, and intensity. Here’s how cyclones affect the monsoon:  Delayed Monsoon Onset  Western Disturbance Disruption: If a cyclone forms in the Arabian Sea during late May or early June, it can disrupt the cross-equatorial flow of moisture-laden winds toward the Indian subcontinent, delaying the southwest monsoon’s arrival. " Example: Cyclone Tauktae (May 2021) delayed the monsoon’s onset in Kerala by over a week due to the diversion of moisture and weakening of low-pressure zones  Early or Accelerated Monsoon Onset  Low-Pressure Boost: Cyclones in the Bay of Bengal can enhance low-pressure areas , pulling monsoon winds toward the Indian coast, accelerating the monsoon’s arrival. " Example: Cyclone Amphan (May 2020) helped advance the monsoon onset over eastern India due to the intense low-pressure system it created.  Uneven Distribution of Rainfall  Localized Intense Rainfall: Cyclones can cause localized heavy rains in coastal areas while reducing rainfall inland , leading to spatial imbalances. " Example: Cyclone Yaas (May 2021) brought torrential rains to Odisha and West Bengal , causing flooding, while northwestern India experienced a rainfall deficit .
